lede: Most joins pair a big table with a small one. If every executor gets its own copy of the small table, the big one never has to be shuffled. That's a broadcast join, and adaptive execution can pick one for you while the query runs.
objectives: Tell a broadcast hash join from a sort-merge join in a physical plan
Control broadcasting with `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` and the `F.broadcast` hint
Explain how adaptive execution (AQE) can switch a join to a broadcast while the query runs
Show that the join strategy changes how Spark works, never which rows you get

blocks.md:
`shipments` has one row per outbound shipment, and each one names its sending warehouse. `warehouses` is small: one row per warehouse. They're loaded as DataFrames, and `F` is `pyspark.sql.functions`.

Spark has two main ways to run an equi-join like `shipments.join(warehouses, "warehouse_id")`:

- **Sort-merge join.** Both sides are shuffled by the key, so matching rows land in the same partition, then each partition is sorted and merged. In a plan you see `SortMergeJoin`, with an `Exchange` under each side.
- **Broadcast hash join.** The small side is collected and a copy is sent to every executor. Each task builds a lookup table from it and streams its part of the big side past it. The big side isn't shuffled at all. In a plan you see `BroadcastHashJoin` and a `BroadcastExchange` over the small side.

Spark broadcasts automatically when its size estimate for one side is under `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold`, 10 MB by default.

blocks.title: Spark broadcasts the small table by itself
blocks.code:
print(spark.conf.get("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold"))
print(spark.conf.get("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled"))

joined = shipments.join(warehouses, on="warehouse_id", how="inner")
plan = joined._jdf.queryExecution().executedPlan().toString()
print("BroadcastHashJoin" in plan, "SortMergeJoin" in plan)
blocks.note: The threshold is 10485760 bytes, which is 10 MB, and adaptive execution is on. The `plan` line, from lessons 55 and 56, gets the physical plan as text, the same text `explain()` prints, so the last line checks which join Spark chose. `warehouses` is a tiny file, so it's a broadcast.

blocks.md:
Settings made with `spark.conf.set` last for the rest of the session. Setting the threshold to `-1` turns automatic broadcasting off.

The next examples also set `spark.sql.adaptive.enabled` to `False`. Adaptive execution can rewrite a plan while it runs (you'll see that below), so switching it off keeps the plan you read the same as the plan that runs.

blocks.title: Automatic broadcast off: a sort-merge join
blocks.code:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", False)
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", -1)

joined = shipments.join(warehouses, on="warehouse_id", how="inner")
plan = joined._jdf.queryExecution().executedPlan().toString()
print("BroadcastHashJoin" in plan, "SortMergeJoin" in plan)
print(plan.count("Exchange hashpartitioning"), "shuffles")
blocks.note: Now both sides are shuffled by `warehouse_id` (two `Exchange hashpartitioning` steps), then sorted and merged. That's fine for two big tables, and wasted work when one side has three rows.

blocks.md:
You know your data better than Spark's estimate. Wrap the small side in `F.broadcast(...)` to ask for a broadcast whatever the threshold says. It's a **hint**: the DataFrame is the same, only marked.

The join strategy never changes the result. Whichever way Spark runs it, an inner join returns the same rows.

blocks.title: The broadcast hint, and the same rows
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", False)
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", -1)

plain = shipments.join(warehouses, "warehouse_id")
hinted = shipments.join(F.broadcast(warehouses), "warehouse_id")
plan = hinted._jdf.queryExecution().executedPlan().toString()
print("BroadcastHashJoin" in plan)

print(sorted(plain.collect()) == sorted(hinted.collect()))
hinted.select("shipment_id", "warehouse_id", "name", "region").orderBy("shipment_id").show()
blocks.note: The hint wins even with automatic broadcasting off. Sorting both lists of rows and comparing them shows the two strategies return exactly the same rows.

blocks.md:
Spark's first plan relies on estimates made before any data is read. **Adaptive query execution** (AQE, on by default) re-plans while the query runs. Each shuffle is a natural pause: when the shuffled data is written, Spark knows its real size. If one side of a sort-merge join turns out to be small enough, AQE switches that join to a broadcast. Its own limit is `spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold`, which follows the main threshold unless you set it.

To see it here, the next example sets the main threshold to a silly 10 bytes, so the first plan has to be a sort-merge join, and gives AQE a normal 10 MB limit. Once the query has run, the plan text has two parts: the final plan, then the initial plan after `== Initial Plan ==`.

blocks.title: AQE switches to a broadcast at run time
blocks.code:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", True)
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", 10)
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "10MB")

joined = shipments.join(warehouses, "warehouse_id")
before = joined._jdf.queryExecution().executedPlan().toString()
print("before running:", "SortMergeJoin" in before, "BroadcastHashJoin" in before)

print(len(joined.collect()), "rows")
after = joined._jdf.queryExecution().executedPlan().toString()
final = after.split("== Initial Plan ==")[0]
print("isFinalPlan=true" in after)
print("final plan:", "BroadcastHashJoin" in final, "SortMergeJoin" in final)
blocks.note: Before it runs, the plan is a sort-merge join. `collect()` runs it, and the plan text now shows what actually ran: after the shuffle, AQE sees how small `warehouses` really is and swaps in a broadcast hash join. Both shuffles had already happened, so the gain is smaller than planning a broadcast from the start; on big data it still saves the sort and spreads the work better.

blocks.md: A broadcast can't go just anywhere. In an outer join, the side whose every row is kept has to be streamed past the lookup table, so only the **other** side can be broadcast. In `shipments.join(..., how="left")` that's the right side. Spark quietly ignores a hint it can't use.

blocks.title: Which side can be broadcast
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", False)
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", -1)

wrong_side = F.broadcast(shipments).join(warehouses, "warehouse_id", "left")
right_side = shipments.join(F.broadcast(warehouses), "warehouse_id", "left")
for name, df in [("hint on shipments", wrong_side), ("hint on warehouses", right_side)]:
    plan = df._jdf.queryExecution().executedPlan().toString()
    print(name, "BroadcastHashJoin" in plan)
blocks.note: With the hint on the kept side, Spark falls back to a sort-merge join. With the hint on `warehouses`, it broadcasts. Either way the rows are the same left join.

blocks.md: Broadcasting doesn't fix a wrong key. `inventory` has one row per **warehouse and SKU**: the same SKU is stocked in several warehouses. To pass more than one key column, give `on` a list: `on=["warehouse_id", "sku"]` matches rows where both are equal, and keeps each key column once.

blocks.title: Broadcast inventory on both keys
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

by_sku = shipments.join(F.broadcast(inventory), on="sku")
by_both = shipments.join(F.broadcast(inventory), on=["warehouse_id", "sku"])
print(by_sku.count(), "rows joined on sku alone")
print(by_both.count(), "rows joined on warehouse and sku")

by_both.select("shipment_id", "warehouse_id", "sku", "quantity", "on_hand").orderBy("shipment_id").show()
blocks.note: SKU-1003 is stocked in three warehouses, so joining on `sku` alone pairs those shipments with every warehouse's stock: 8 rows from 4 shipments. With both keys each shipment meets only its own warehouse's row.

concept.prompt: `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` is `-1` and you write `shipments.join(F.broadcast(warehouses), "warehouse_id")`. What does Spark do?
choices: A sort-merge join, because automatic broadcasting is off
A broadcast hash join: the hint asks for it whatever the threshold says
It raises an error about the threshold
concept.why: The threshold only controls automatic broadcasting. `F.broadcast` is a hint Spark follows when the join type allows it.

concept.prompt: The same inner join runs once as a broadcast hash join and once as a sort-merge join. How do the results compare?
choices: The broadcast join drops rows that don't fit in memory
The sort-merge join returns its rows sorted by the key, so the results differ
They hold exactly the same rows; only the way Spark does the work differs
The broadcast join can return duplicate rows
concept.why: The join strategy is a physical choice. It changes shuffles and memory use, never which rows come back. Neither strategy promises a row order.

concept.prompt: Why can adaptive execution switch a sort-merge join to a broadcast when the first plan couldn't?
choices: It reads the whole table into the driver before planning
After a shuffle stage runs, it knows the real size of the data instead of an estimate
It always broadcasts the right side
concept.why: AQE re-plans at shuffle boundaries using the measured size of the shuffled data. If one side is small enough, it swaps in a broadcast hash join.

review: A broadcast hash join copies the small side to every executor, so the big side isn't shuffled. A sort-merge join shuffles and sorts both sides.
Spark broadcasts automatically below `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` (10 MB by default); `-1` turns that off.
`F.broadcast(df)` is a hint: it asks for a broadcast whatever the threshold. In an outer join only the side that isn't kept whole can be broadcast.
Adaptive execution re-plans after each shuffle with real sizes, and can switch a sort-merge join to a broadcast while the query runs.
Check the strategy with the plan text, for example `"BroadcastHashJoin" in plan`. Set adaptive execution explicitly when the plan matters.
The strategy never changes the rows. Get the keys right first: `on=["warehouse_id", "sku"]` joins on both.
